initial_requirements: Owners and users of a computing cluster need a scheduler that allocates processing resources according to user-oriented quality-of-service goals. Libra will receive submitted batch jobs from an existing cluster management system and schedule them using information such as each user's budget and deadline. It should select suitable execution resources and enforce the resulting allocation while the surrounding platform remains responsible for receiving and dispatching jobs.

messages.content: Hello, I'm GPTREI, your requirements elicitation assistant. Today, I’ll be gathering detailed information about your needs for the Libra Economy-Driven Cluster Scheduler to make sure we understand the requirements clearly. Before we begin, are you in line with the scope of this interview, or do your expectations differ?

Yes, that sounds in line with what I’m expecting. I’m here to talk through how Libra should make scheduling decisions based on things like budget and deadline, and how it should fit alongside the existing cluster management system.
Thank you. To start off, could you please introduce yourself and your connection to this project?

I’m representing the operations side of the cluster environment, so I’m concerned with how jobs get scheduled fairly and efficiently for different users. My interest is making sure Libra helps meet user service goals without disrupting the rest of the platform.
Thanks for that context. Could you describe the current process or system you use today for submitting, scheduling, and running batch jobs in the cluster?

Today, users submit batch jobs through our existing cluster management system, and that platform handles the intake and dispatching. Scheduling is much more traditional, mostly based on whatever resources are available rather than on user-specific service goals like budget or deadlines. We want Libra to sit in that flow and make the allocation decision before execution without taking over the whole submission pipeline.
What current processes do you want Libra to change or improve, or what are the main features you hope to get from this project?

We want Libra to make scheduling more goal-driven, so jobs can be placed with the user’s budget and deadline in mind instead of just first-come, first-served. It should choose appropriate execution resources and enforce that allocation so users get predictable outcomes. The main improvement is better alignment between what the user is willing to spend and when they need the result.
Are there any other features you would like to see in Libra, perhaps something like user notifications, reporting, or handling cases where budget and deadline goals conflict?

Conflict handling is definitely important, because sometimes a job won’t be able to meet both goals at once. In those cases, I’d want Libra to make a sensible tradeoff and be able to explain, at least at a basic level, why a job was scheduled the way it was. Notifications and reporting would be useful too, but I’d treat those as secondary unless they’re needed for users to understand delays or overruns.
Based on your description, do you think Libra should also include a mechanism to reject or defer jobs when no allocation can satisfy the budget or deadline constraints?

Yes, I think it should have that capability. If no viable allocation exists, Libra shouldn’t just force something arbitrary; it should either reject the job or defer it with a clear reason so users know why it couldn’t be scheduled under their constraints. That would be better than silently violating the budget or missing the deadline without warning.

So far, the main features seem to be: goal-driven scheduling using budget and deadline, selecting and enforcing suitable execution resources, handling budget/deadline conflicts with sensible tradeoffs and explanations, and rejecting or deferring jobs when constraints can’t be met, with notifications/reporting as secondary support. Is that an accurate summary?

Yes, that’s an accurate summary of what I’ve described. The only thing I’d add is that Libra needs to fit cleanly into the existing cluster management flow, since it’s making the scheduling decision but not replacing the whole submission and dispatch system.
Which of these features should be highest priority for the first version of Libra?

The highest priority for the first version should be the core scheduling decision based on budget and deadline, plus enforcing the selected allocation. If we can’t do that reliably, the rest doesn’t matter much. After that, the ability to reject or defer jobs when constraints can’t be met would be the next most important piece.
Please elaborate on what you want Libra’s budget- and deadline-based scheduling decision to accomplish in practice.

In practice, I want Libra to look at each submitted job and decide whether it can be run in a way that stays within the user’s budget while still meeting the deadline. If there are multiple ways to do that, it should choose the most suitable one based on the job’s needs and available cluster resources. The main point is that users get a predictable outcome tied to their priorities, rather than an arbitrary placement.
How should Libra behave when there is no allocation that can satisfy both the budget and the deadline?

If both can’t be satisfied, Libra should not guess or silently stretch one of the constraints. It should either choose the better tradeoff if that is allowed by policy, or reject or defer the job and clearly indicate which constraint could not be met. I’d want that behavior to be consistent so users can trust the scheduler’s decisions.
Could you describe what “better tradeoff” means in your environment—should Libra prioritize budget over deadline, deadline over budget, or follow a policy you define per job or user?

I’d prefer it to follow a policy that can vary per user or even per job, because not everyone values the same thing. For some workloads, meeting the deadline is critical even if it costs more, while for others staying within budget matters more than finishing early. If there has to be a default, I’d lean toward deadline first for time-sensitive jobs and budget first for routine batch work, but I’d want that to be configurable.

What should Libra use as the basis for choosing suitable execution resources—do you already have resource attributes or constraints in mind, such as machine type, cost, performance, or reservation availability?

Yes, cost and performance are the main ones I’d expect Libra to consider first, along with whether a resource is actually available when the job needs it. Machine type matters too, but mostly as a way to capture differences in capacity or speed rather than as a user-facing rule by itself. If there are reservation or queueing constraints in the cluster, Libra should respect those as part of the decision.
To keep the interview concise, I’d like to ask one final question: who else do you think has valuable insights into Libra’s requirements, and whose needs or concerns should we also consider?

The cluster operators will have important input, especially around feasibility, enforcement, and what kinds of resource controls they can actually support. I’d also include the users who submit jobs, because they’ll care about predictability, pricing, and how failures or deferrals are explained. If there are finance or capacity-planning stakeholders, their perspective would help too since the whole system is tied to budgets and utilization.
